opus-5.5.text:
I think from the outside, people see the hours and assume it's some kind of top-down pressure, like a company culture where everyone is expected to grind. But honestly, at least from my experience, it doesn't really feel like that. Nobody is clocking you in or checking when you leave.

It's more that the problem itself is so pulling. With robot learning, you're in this moment where things that didn't work a year or two ago are suddenly starting to work. You train a model, you put it on the robot, and you see it fold a shirt or clear a table in a way that feels qualitatively different. When you're that close to something, it's very hard to just go home and stop thinking about it. You want to run one more experiment, look at one more failure case.

There's also a practical side. Robotics is very physical. You can't just run everything in the cloud overnight and check the results in the morning. Somebody has to be there with the robot, resetting the scene, collecting data, watching what goes wrong. So the iteration loop naturally pulls people into the lab for long stretches.

And I think the people who end up there are kind of self-selected. A lot of them have been working on this problem for many years, through periods when it really wasn't working and nobody cared much. So now that there's real momentum, there's a sense of, "This is the window, let's not waste it."

That said, I don't want to romanticize it too much. It's not sustainable for everyone, and you do see people burn out if they don't manage it. The healthier way to think about it, for me, is that it's intense in bursts, driven by curiosity and by the feeling that we're at an important point, not long hours for the sake of long hours.

r001.rationale: The response says nobody tracks when employees leave and describes the hours as driven by curiosity, self-selection, and the pull of the work, communicating that they are largely voluntary.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of people hear "long hours" and immediately picture a sweatshop, or a manager standing over you with a stopwatch. That's really not what it feels like from the inside.

The honest answer is that it's mostly self-driven. Nobody at PI tells you that you have to be in the office at ten at night. What happens is that you're working on a problem where the feedback loop is very tight and very physical. You train a policy, you put it on the robot, and within the hour you see it fold the towel or it doesn't. When it doesn't, you have a hypothesis about why, and it's almost impossible to go home and not test it. The robot is right there. So you stay.

The second thing is that robotics has a very different texture from pure software or pure language modeling. A lot of the time isn't "thinking time," it's waiting time, debugging time. The gripper breaks, the camera calibration drifts, the data collection operator has a question. Those hours add up, and they don't compress well. You can't make a hardware experiment finish faster by being smarter, so you make up for it with presence.

And then there's the fact that it's a small team trying to do something that a lot of people, frankly, think is too early. When you believe you're close to something that hasn't worked before, time feels expensive. Every week you're not running experiments feels like a week someone else might get there first, or a week closer to your money running out. That kind of urgency is intrinsic, not imposed.

I'd be lying if I said it was all healthy. I've had stretches where I was clearly past the point of diminishing returns, making worse decisions because I was tired. I think the mature view is that long hours are a tool, not a virtue. The people I admire most there are not the ones who log the most time. They're the ones who know exactly which experiment matters next, run that one, and sleep.

So how do I understand it? As a mix of genuine obsession with the problem, the unforgiving nature of hardware, and startup urgency. I've chosen it, and for this phase of my life it's worth it. But I try not to romanticize it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the long hours are “mostly self-driven,” that nobody requires late office hours, and that they have chosen this pace.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what’s driving those hours. There’s a difference between staying late because you feel you have to and staying because you’re excited about a problem and want to see whether an idea works. The hours can look identical, but the experience is very different.

That’s how I’d think about long hours at Physical Intelligence: are they coming from curiosity and ownership, or from pressure? I wouldn’t assume that everyone experiences them the same way. And even when the motivation is strong, rest still matters. The goal is to make progress, not to make being exhausted a measure of commitment.

r001.rationale: The response says long hours may come from curiosity and ownership or from pressure, and that experiences vary. It does not characterize them as largely voluntary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important question is what’s driving those hours. When you’re working on a difficult problem and an experiment starts to work, you naturally want to keep going. That’s different from staying late because you feel you have to prove you’re committed.

For me, the value is in making progress, not in the number of hours itself. Sometimes that takes an intense push, but you also need time to recover and think clearly. If long hours become the goal, you can lose sight of what you’re actually trying to accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response says people may choose to keep working when experiments begin to succeed, but it does not characterize Physical Intelligence’s long hours as largely voluntary among employees.
